summary: Discovery focused on unit economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Customer cares about per-token pricing, batching and caching levers, predictable monthly caps, and security (VPC/KMS). Agreed next steps: share pricing grid, benchmarking plan, sample prompts, schedule technical deep dive.
topics: Current stack and workloads (text generation + embeddings)
Batching, KV/prefix caching, and autoscaling impacts
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
transcript: 00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, AE, with Priya our SE. How's it going?
00:05 Mark: Hey Jordan, good, thanks. We have about 40 minutes. Wanted to jump into the cost econ stuff — our CFO is nervous about token costs at scale.
00:12 Jordan: Totally — that's the point of today's call. Quick context from you on workloads?

00:18 Mark: We're running a mix of long-form generation for reports (~1k-3k tokens), chat assistants (200-800 tokens), and embeddings for retrieval. Monthly token volume target is about 1.2B tokens but we expect 3x growth in 6 months if the pilot goes well.
00:35 Priya: Nice — and are those real-time user-facing latencies or async batch jobs?
00:40 Sarah: Mostly real-time for chat, need sub-300ms 95p for short chats. For long-form generation we can tolerate a sec or two. Embeddings are async bulk jobs overnight.
00:52 Jordan: Got it. So main constraints: per-token cost budget, tail latency for chat, and predictable monthly spend. Is there any compliance requirement?
00:59 Tom: We need SOC2 level audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration. Also prefer data to stay in our VPC for some PII workflows — so private deployment might be required for that subset.

01:12 Jordan: Perfect — that's common. On pricing: Redwood hosted per-token is usage-based; dedicated is a reserved capacity model (monthly commit plus lower unit token cost). Private adds platform fees plus infra. Priya, want to run through the unit math?

01:25 Priya: Sure. Super high-level: hosted is simplest — you pay per-token and we manage everything; you pay a premium but no committed spend. Dedicated has two pieces: a reservation (monthly) to get dev/ops isolation and lower per-token egress. The interesting levers are batching and prefix/KV caching — they materially reduce cost per token on high-reuse workloads.
01:45 Mark: When you say caching, you mean KV cache for generation, prefix cache for common prompts? We've got a lot of RAG where users hit similar documents.

01:52 Priya: Exactly — you can cache prefixes and commonly used KV states; that reduces the compute per token because you don't recompute attentions for cached parts. Also batching across concurrent requests helps improve GPU utilization, lowering cost per token. We can show example numbers.

02:05 Jordan: For example, for a typical 8k model on hosted, list price is X per 1k prompt tokens and Y per 1k completion tokens — but with caching/batching for your mix, effective cost can drop 20-40% depending on hit rates. On dedicated, after commit, unit cost can be another 30-50% lower than hosted list.
02:28 Mark: Can you be more concrete? Our CFO expects a per-1M-token cost estimate for chat and for long-form. Right now we pay with another provider and cost is a blocker.

02:36 Priya: Sure — we can model it. Quick sketch (very rough): hosted short-chat effective cost ~ $0.80-1.20 per 1k tokens at low caching, long-form maybe $0.6-1.0 per 1k depending on model. With caching + batching on dedicated, you can see $0.3-0.6 per 1k. These are illustrative, we'll share a full grid. The driver is GPU occupancy and number of tokens generated per GPU-second.
02:58 Sarah: That spread seems big — what assumptions? batch sizes, concurrency?

03:02 Priya: Right. For chat we assume low-latency SLOs so we have smaller batches and more reserved capacity. If your 95p needs <300ms then batch sizes are constrained. If you can accept 500ms, we can batch more aggressively and lower unit cost. For long-form, higher batching and caching are possible since latency tolerance is higher.
03:18 Tom: For dedicated, what's the commitment level and how do we size? We don't want to overcommit and waste money.

03:24 Jordan: Commit is monthly GPU pool size equivalent. We size it based on your peak concurrency and token throughput. We recommend starting with a modest commit and use autoscale/burst policy to handle spikes. Billing is blended: commit covers baseline capacity; bursts are billed at dedicated-on-demand rates.
03:38 Mark: Any tooling to estimate sizing from our logs? We currently have usage from our dev env and some prod traces.
03:43 Priya: Yes — send sample traces, we run a sizing exercise and give a forecast. We'll also produce a benchmark that replicates your token distribution across model sizes and context lengths.
03:52 Sarah: About private deployment: does private mean completely customer-managed infra or is it a hybrid with a control plane?

03:58 Jordan: It's a hybrid. Control plane can be in Redwood but with VPC peering and private networking; or fully on-prem with customer-managed control plane if air-gapped. Private adds platform fee and extra ops work but gives full network isolation and KMS integration.
04:10 Tom: And does private affect per-token runtime cost? Like are kernels optimized differently?

04:14 Priya: The runtime is the same, but if you're managing infra, your infra costs (GPU instances, networking) are external. Redwood can provide guidance on instance types and optimized quantization profiles. We also support our compiled kernels and batching logic across environments, so performance is comparable.
04:29 Mark: We talked about 8k vs 32k contexts. Does longer context increase token cost linearly?

04:34 Priya: Not strictly linear — inference compute increases with context length (attention cost), but prefix caching helps. If you frequently reuse long prefixes, the marginal cost per request drops a lot. For one-off long contexts, cost per token is higher because attention scales O(n^2) for some model parts, but our optimizations mitigate that.
04:50 Mark: Any ballpark on caching hit rates you typically see for RAG?

04:53 Priya: It varies — for corpora with repeated intros/outlines we see 30-60% effective token reduction on generation; for retrieval-heavy RAG it's lower unless you canonicalize prompts. We'll benchmark with your sample prompts.

05:03 Jordan: Also worth noting function/tool calls and streaming affect billing patterns — streaming reduces perceived latency but can change per-token accounting slightly depending on how tokens are emitted.
05:12 Mark: Good. What's the break-even point where dedicated becomes cheaper than hosted?

05:15 Priya: There's a simple formula: if expected monthly token volume and concurrency exceed a threshold (depends on model family and SLO), dedicated wins. For your 1.2B tokens/month projected to 3.6B in 6 months, dedicated is almost certainly better economically, assuming a moderate commit and good caching. We'll compute the threshold in the pricing spreadsheet.
05:33 Sarah: Are there minimum terms for Dedicated?
05:36 Jordan: Monthly commits are typical; discounts for annual. We can do trials/pilots with short-term reserved pools to gather real metrics before a long-term commit.
05:44 Tom: On security, we need KMS + audit logs. Are those standard on Dedicated and Private?
05:49 Jordan: Yes — Dedicated and Private include KMS integration and audit logs, and we can support SAML/SSO. We'll attach SOC2 docs in the follow-up link.
05:58 Mark: Awesome. Can you also show example per-case bills — e.g., 1M short-chat tokens vs 100k long-form requests?
06:04 Priya: Yes — we'll produce sample invoices and unit economics, plus sensitivity to caching hit rate and batch size. We'll include a runbook for changing batch sizes vs SLOs.
06:12 Sarah: One more: what about autoscaling latency during spikes? We can't have user-facing errors during market hours.

06:18 Priya: We do warm pools and burst capacity; routing policies can failover to a lower-cost model variant or region. For critical traffic you can pin to dedicated nodes with headroom reserved. We'll propose SLO-aware autoscale config in the plan.
06:29 Mark: Any gotchas around tokenization differences? We use a custom tokenizer in our data pipeline.

06:33 Priya: Tokenization differences can change token counts by ~5-15% depending on language. We recommend standardizing or sending a sample to size accurately. We'll accept your tokenizer artifacts for bench runs.
06:45 Jordan: Ok let's do a quick recap of next steps — we'll send the pricing grid, benchmark plan, and schedule a deep dive. Anything else?
06:52 Tom: Please include an example pilot scope and what success metrics you measure — cost per 1k tokens, 95p latency, cache hit rate.
06:58 Jordan: Will do. We'll also propose a 2-week pilot to run against your sample prompts and return measured unit costs.
07:03 Mark: Sounds good. One minor note — our procurement wants a clear cancellation policy for Dedicated, are there penalties?
07:08 Jordan: Standard terms vary; short pilots have no long-term penalties. For committed contracts we have early termination clauses; we'll route legal to procurement if you want term specifics.
07:18 Sarah: Could you share the SOC2 doc now or in the follow-up?
07:21 Jordan: We'll attach it in the follow-up email along with the pricing spreadsheet link (drive link: https://redwood.app/pricing-grid — placeholder).
07:28 Priya: I'll also include a sample benchmark script and infra sizing worksheet.
07:33 Mark: Great — thanks, folks. We'll review and send prompts. Any other closing notes?
07:37 Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by Friday with docs and calendar invite for the technical deep dive next week.
07:42 Tom: Appreciate it, bye.
07:43 Mark: Thanks, bye.
07:44 Sarah: Bye.
notes: Transcript shows realistic ASR imperfections and occasional short timestamps; speakers sometimes overlap. References made to benchmark artifacts and a shared pricing sheet link. Customer leaning toward Dedicated given growth projection but requires a pilot and procurement terms.
